turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell asked Jack for the address of his country residence and inquired about the number of servants he employed there.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that his country residence was located in Hertfordshire, and he employed four servants.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell asked Jack for the names and ages of his house staff and inquired whether his residence had been built before the Great Fire of London, as she considered only houses from that era respectable.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that the names of his house staff were Mrs. Stabbins, the housekeeper, Mr. Snooks, the butler, and two footmen named Thomas and William. He added that his residence had been built after the Great Fire of London but noted that it was still quite respectable.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell asked Jack if he had any ancestral portraits and inquired about his family connections, as she believed a lack of ancestral connections was a serious deficiency in a young man.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he did not have any ancestral portraits but mentioned that his father had been a captain in the Royal Navy and that he had several cousins who were quite well-regarded in society.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell asked Jack about his financial situation and inquired whether he had any immediate prospects of inheriting a fortune, as she believed it was essential for a gentleman to have a substantial income.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he was currently managing an estate and hoped to secure further financial stability through his work and investments.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell asked Jack if he had any immediate prospects of a title or at least a baronetcy, as she considered these distinctions essential for any gentleman aspiring to marry into her family.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that while he did not currently hold any titles, he was committed to working hard and hoped to earn the respect of society through his efforts and contributions.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell asked Jack if he had any connections to the aristocracy or influential families, as she believed such associations were crucial for a gentleman's social standing.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that although he did not have any direct connections to the aristocracy, he was committed to making valuable contributions to society and hoped to earn the respect of influential circles through his hard work and dedication.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that while his intentions were commendable, she could not overlook the importance of established connections and social standing. She asked if he had any acquaintances among the nobility or influential figures who could vouch for his character and capabilities.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that although he lacked such connections at present, he was determined to prove himself through his actions and hoped that his efforts would eventually earn him the respect and recognition he sought.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that while her approval was contingent upon his ability to secure a respectable position, she found his current aspirations somewhat lacking in practicality and connection to the upper echelons of society.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he understood her concerns and would work diligently to build connections that would strengthen his social standing, hoping to meet her high standards in the future.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen told her mother that she found Jack's determination admirable and hoped that his future accomplishments would earn the respect of all, including her.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that while she appreciated his ambition, the current circumstances were not satisfactory and that he must strive to align himself with the right circles to secure her daughter’s future. She also asked Gwendolen to consider more carefully the nature of the connections and respectability required in her choice of a husband.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he understood her requirements and would strive to meet them, promising to work towards the connections and respectability she deemed necessary.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that she would continue to monitor his progress closely and that any deviation from the path of social respectability would not be tolerated. She also reminded Gwendolen of the importance of marrying within their class and ensuring the family's continued prominence.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell that she was engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen that she was not engaged to anyone and that when she did become engaged, she or her father would inform her of the fact.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell, 'Mamma!'

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen to go to the carriage.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen to get into the carriage.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack to take a seat.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he preferred standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that she felt bound to inform him that he was not down on her list of eligible young men.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he must admit he smoked.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that she was glad to hear it and that a man should always have an occupation of some kind.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he was twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Jack if he knew everything or nothing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he knew nothing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that she was pleased to hear it and that she did not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that his income was between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Jack if his income was in land or in investments.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that his income was in investments.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that it was satisfactory.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he had a country house with some land attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that a country house was satisfactory and asked how many bedrooms it had.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he owned a house in Belgrave Square, but it was let by the year to Lady Bloxham.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that she did not know Lady Bloxham.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that Lady Bloxham went about very little and was a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that nowadays that was no guarantee of respectability of character and asked what number in Belgrave Square.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that the number was 149.
